en: Divine power will bring before you
The person you saw in your dream.
In the dream you dreamed asleep,
The sharp Albar sword you girded
Is a gift bestowed by God.
According to the traditions,
And if you ask the wise,
It is the heirloom handed down
As a gift from his forefather, gray-maned Manas,
That mighty and sagacious hero,
Among all sons born of humankind,
The one unmatched champion.
His given name is Akjoltoy;
Alone, he is worth a host.
His breadth is like a sprawling valley,
His keenness is like steel;
God has granted your desire.
The answer to your longing,
Joltoy, has come bearing news.
If a swift steed was tied at your post,
You mounted your destined fortune.
The keen Albar sword that cleaves stone
Is your kinsman Joltoy himself;
It means the panther’s hour of coming has arrived.
If a falcon alighted at your ford,
It means your destined road lies there.
God has opened the way to your fortune,
And the enemy who opposed you has fled.
Sister, if you dream while sleeping
That your fortune opened in the marketplace,
Your sustenance, luck, and prosperity
Have spread across the face of the earth.
May destiny bring before you
The panther, the hero Seytek.
If, while sleeping in your dream,
You behold a place akin to paradise,
Holding the sun in your left hand
And seeing the moon in your right,
Your wish has been granted,
And the one you watched for has come.
Your abundant fortune has opened,
And the wonder in which you were immersed,
The lion Seytek himself,
Was the moon you lay embracing.
If the sun was in your left hand,
Your prosperity and fortune are on their way.
One who does not burn when cast into fire,
Whom a sword cannot cut,
Who does not sink when cast into water,
Who yields his wisdom to no mortal,
Whom no man can defeat in combat,
The solid core of tempered steel—
That panther, the hero Seytek,
Will be, dear sister,
The father of your male offspring.
If you saw a true eagle in your dream,
The one who subdues all fanged beasts,
The one who throws the world into tumult,
Is the lion Seytek himself.
If you rode a chestnut horse,
Your treasure was Seytek’s possession.
You will be immersed in delight;
He has come to meet your destiny,
And you will play without growing weary.
If you went hunting and flew your bird,
And took both lions and tigers,
It is a manifest gift from God;
Is it not your gray-maned Seytek?
All the fanged beasts,
Startled from their noble pride,
Unable to bear his awesome might,
Fled in every direction;
This means the hero Seytek
Is your lion, like his father.
With the spirit of Manas supporting him,
Every one of his enemies
The young panther Seytek
Will trample beneath his feet.
Against the Black Chinese and the Manchus,
He will march and attack the khan;
In time, his deeds will become an epic.”
Perizada Külayım
Thus interpreted the dream.
Saying, “May your dream come true,”
She brought her words to an end.
When Akbermet heard this,
She swiftly cried, “Baabedin!”
To the spirit of Manas
She dedicated a moon-hoofed horse,
Slaughtered a double-humped camel,
And a mare whose udder was a span wide.
In a copper cauldron with golden handles,
She boiled and cooked the meat,
Spreading out all her wealth.
Her heart surged and her blood boiled within;
Bermet was so excited she could not keep still.
From the city of the fairies,
From the settlement she had brought along,
Among the companions of her own age,
Among radiant, exceedingly lovely women,
Who walked and played together,
Confidantes skilled in conversation,
Had she not brought with her
Eighty young wives and eighty maidens,
Companions who dispelled her sorrow?
Their waists were handspans, their faces like the moon,
They were serene beauties,
Radiant faces without a single mole.
The heart turned toward them at a glance;
Their beauty was fashioned unlike any other.
Half were wives and half were maidens,
With thimble mouths and camel-calf eyes,
No wicked word ever passed their lips.
Whoever saw them
Lost his senses and grew bewildered.
Every living soul
Felt as though its deepest thirst were quenched.
Their faces were smooth and flawless as candles;
In Bermet, daughter of the fairies,
Every imaginable beauty could be found.
Those coquettish, hapless beauties,
Their breasts like tightly knotted silk,
If a living soul gazed upon them,
Even the dead would burn with longing.
Their hair was like sable fur,
Such as a fortunate man would love.
If their hands happened to touch him,
A man’s heart would take wing like a bird,
And he would laugh and play without a care.
The unfortunate queen Bermet,
Whose wisdom surpassed most,
Turned toward the skilled women
And gave orders to the maidens.
The maidens did not stand idly by,
Nor did they disobey her command,
But delighted the hearts of all who saw them.
Upon plane trees towering beyond sight,
They formed equal groups of six
And had swings hung,
Until games and laughter thundered,
And the clamor split the sky.
In groups of six, each party
Walked side by side in rows;
Such was their splendid display,
A wondrous spectacle to behold.
To satisfy the hearts of all who saw,
Across a low blue-mottled hill
They spread the carpet of fortune.
Such was the carpet’s nature:
Rubies and precious jewels
Were strewn along its edges.
Yellow gold, like a reclining camel,
Was shaped into the figure of a tiger
And set in its center.
Countless costly treasures
Had been lavishly worked into it.
Anyone who gazed upon it
Was utterly robbed of his senses.
Carpets of that kind
Were fashioned in many designs.
That very carpet
Had been soaked in water for forty years;
Not even its patterned edge had faded.
If left damp for eighty days,
Its border did not rot.
Bearskins and tiger hides
Were spread as splendid mats.
Whoever stood gazing upon them
Feasted his eyes to his heart’s content.
The wealth of that serene beauty
Dazzled the eyes.
How many forms her riches took!
The treasures spread across the field
Looked like radiant paradise.
The wealth of Bermet, daughter of the fairies,
Was poured forth in abundance.
Like a prince beloved by the people,
She had spread out her riches
As though expecting honored guests.
From costly treasures
She had heaped up mounds.
To the unfortunate woman,
Wealth had been given without measure.
Eighty wives and eighty maidens
Played the game of Orompoy;
The clamor of their swinging
Rang out in a ceaseless roar.
Just then the hero Seytek,
That dear lion bold as a rooster,
The steadfast gray-maned hero,
Clasped his hands behind his back
And sighed as though weary,
Then summoned his muraas.
The six champions who tended his horses,
Warriors skilled against the foe,
The finest of his companions,
Would seize anyone who defied them
And hurl him down upon the ground.
When told to advance, they never turned back;
They expertly speared the enemy,
Their heavy muskets strapped upon them.
At the cry of “Charge!” they rushed with a roar,
All equally prepared for battle.
Warriors never sated with blood,
Panther-like, gray-maned champions.
Skilled in drawing the bow,
Master marksmen who never missed.
Each lion had a different bearing,
Hotheads capable of shattering the world.
The cause of their fierce temper was this:
Born of women who gazed upon true men,
They had come into the world as genuine heroes,
Making slaves of those they fixed their eyes upon,
And dealing punishment with their own hands.
They surged forward like wild boars,
And prowled like tigers.
When Seytek gave the command,
They mingled dust with dust.
When black muskets cracked,
They fought without tiring.
When a surging flood of blood advanced,
They stood beneath the banner.
When the fierce musket snapped,
They fought without flinching.
When waves of enemy troops approached,
Each one slaughtered a thousand.
If a mountain-covering flood came,
They stood firm and barred its way.
Throwing it head over heels,
They dashed the tiger to the ground.
If gray-maned Seytek commanded,
“Drink water,” they would drink poison;
“Take his cap,” they would cut off his head;
“Spill blood,” they would spill their very souls.
Those mighty men were ready to strike the foe;
When all were roused to fury,
Their strength could overcome multitudes.
Like great morning stars in stature,
All the companions of fortunate hero Seytek
Were heroes themselves.
They were born for valor,
And marched together against the foe.
And whenever their fury seized them,
They drove giants into the earth.
Through broad ravines where no bird flew,
They sounded brass pipes beneath silken canopies;
Through broad ravines where no water flowed,
They sounded trumpets of brass.
At that moment the gray-maned lion,
And all his well-honed warriors,
Ran as swiftly as arrows in flight,
Spending every last breath in their haste.
All the gray-maned champions together
Showed their nimble prowess.
Once the hero’s command had come,
They said, “Today the road shall be open,”
